transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-09-29 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Lara (OrionBridge Head of ML), Diego (Infra Lead), Priya (Procurement)

Summary/Agenda: quick intros, understand OrionBridge usage patterns and budget constraints, explain per-token economics and levers (batching, caching, quantization/residency), define pilot scope and next steps.

00:00 Maya Thompson: Hi everyone, thanks for making time. quick round robin, then we'll jump into the economics.
00:15 Lara Chen: Hi, Lara here. we run inference for customer support summarization and a small assistant. about 120k requests/day right now, peak bursts midday, um, pretty sensitive to 95th/99th latency.
00:28 Diego Ramos: Diego — infra — we have a GCP tenancy and some on-prem hardware for regulated customers. data residency is a must for EU contracts.
00:40 Ethan Park: cool, thanks. quick clarifying q — when you say 120k requests, is that single-turn or with histories?
00:50 Lara Chen: mostly single turn but we do pass a 200–400 token context for some flows. average output is 150 tokens.
01:05 Maya Thompson: okay good. so that's the basis for token math. we'll walk through hosted vs dedicated vs private cost levers and then show how batching and KV prefix caching change unit cost.
02:10 Lara Chen: budget wise — our finance told us roughly $60k/month for inference across all models; that's a hard cap for the next 6 months while we validate.
02:25 Priya Nair: and procurement needs SOC2 + data residency papers before we can sign anything.
02:35 Maya Thompson: understood. we have SOC 2 docs, and we can scope a dedicated tenancy or VPC with customer-managed keys.
03:00 Ethan Park: small note — when teams say KV cache we sometimes see it pronounced K-V cash — not that it matters, but I want to— there are two effects: prefix cache that reduces repeated context cost and KV cache which speeds autoregressive decoding by avoiding re-computation. both can materially lower per-token spend.
03:38 Diego Ramos: could you ballpark the delta? like hosted vs dedicated per token?
03:45 Maya Thompson: yeah ballpark — depends on model and qps but think hosted is lowest up-front because it's usage-based; per-token price can be a bit higher because of multi-tenant overhead. dedicated is more about predictable throughput — unit cost often drops once you reach sustained usage and can benefit from quantization profiles we recommend. private/on-prem usually has highest ops overhead but gives residency and cost control long term.
04:12 Lara Chen: can you give numbers for our profile — 200 token input + 150 token output mean ~350 tokens per request, 120k/day?
04:25 Ethan Park: quick calc — 120k * 350 = 42M tokens/day. multiply by 30 yields ~1.26B tokens/month. big enough to make dedicated interesting.
04:40 Maya Thompson: exactly. at that token volume a dedicated pool with conservative batching can reduce per-token effective cost by 20–40% vs hosted, depending on how much we can batch and cache.
05:05 Lara Chen: but we can't increase latency more than 300ms p95 on the assistant flows.
05:12 Ethan Park: that's a useful SLO. batching helps throughput, but larger batch windows increase tail latency. we can do adaptive batching: small windows for latency-sensitive routes and larger windows for batch-y work. Redwood's routing can split traffic across policies.
06:00 Diego Ramos: how mature is the adaptive batching? is it per-route?
06:10 Ethan Park: yes per-route. you can set a target p95 and cost priority. the runtime will attempt to respect latency SLOs while maximizing batching. in practice we see 2–3x throughput gain on the batch-friendly routes without violating p95.
07:00 Lara Chen: what about KV cache — our logs show a lot of repeated system prompts across users. could that reduce token consumption?
07:12 Maya Thompson: absolutely. prefix caching can avoid re-sending the system prompt each time and reduce tokens sent to the model. amortized savings depend on how much of the prompt is static. if you have a 200-token system prompt and it's repeated, that's big wins. KV cache reduces compute per token rather than tokens billed — but that also lowers cost on dedicated because it reduces GPU cycles.
08:00 Priya Nair: procurement Q — on hosted, do you provide audit logs, retention windows? we need 12 months of auditability for EU customers.
08:15 Maya Thompson: hosted includes audit logs and can get extended retention as an add-on; dedicated / private give you more control over retention policies and direct log shipping to your SIEM.
09:00 Lara Chen: earlier you said quantization — can that break our accuracy? we rely on factuality for some flows.
09:12 Ethan Park: good question. quantization profiles are workload dependent. we run evals on your prompt/eval set to recommend FP16 or 4-bit quantization variants; sometimes there's a small drop in rare edge cases, we monitor via eval regressions. Redwood Optimize can flag regressions on your evaluation prompts.
10:00 Diego Ramos: about residency — if we go dedicated in a region but data residency required in EU, is redis of keys a blocker?
10:10 Maya Thompson: we support customer-managed KMS in region, and Private (VPC/On-prem) modes can be fully inside your network. there are extra ops steps for on-prem but doable.
11:00 Lara Chen: for the pilot, we want to validate cost per effective response at our traffic profile. what should the pilot look like?
11:10 Maya Thompson: two parts: 1) a pricing pilot — we give you a month of test compute or discounted dedicated capacity + detailed per-token breakouts; 2) a KV/batching sim — run your sample prompts through Redwood runtime to show latency and token/billing deltas. we usually do a 2–4 week pilot.
12:00 Priya Nair: timeline: procurement can do a 30-day review, but we'll need SOC2 attachments and a short SOW.
12:30 Maya Thompson: we'll attach SOC2 and an SOW template.
13:00 Lara Chen: can you run the KV cache sim with our sample prompts? we'll share them after the call.
13:10 Ethan Park: yes, if you share the prompt set and expected session patterns I can run the sim and produce a sensitivity table: per-token billed, effective compute, p95 latency under different batching windows and cache hit rates.
14:00 Diego Ramos: what's the expected reduction if we hit a 70% cache-hit on the common system prompt?
14:12 Ethan Park: rough thumb — if 200 tokens per request are static and you get 70% hit, tokens billed per request could drop by ~140 tokens so effective tokens per request could go from 350 to ~210, that's ~40% token reduction. compute reduction depends on cache type — prefix cache mostly saves billed tokens; KV cache speeds decoding and can reduce GPU utilization by another 10–20% depending on model.
15:30 Lara Chen: wow that's significant. ok then the pilot is attractive.
16:00 Maya Thompson: pricing note — for hosted we quote simple per-token; for dedicated we can do a blended model: capacity commit + overage per-token. private is typically a license plus support and then infra cost. I'll include three rows in the pilot pricing spreadsheet with example numbers for your monthly token volumes.
17:00 Priya Nair: procurement likes examples. please include contract length sensitivity (month-to-month vs annual) and cancellation terms.
17:12 Maya Thompson: will do.
18:00 Diego Ramos: any notable limitations with model variants — like tiny quantized variants for latency-sensitive endpoints?
18:15 Ethan Park: yes we have quantized variants that run faster; there's an accuracy vs latency trade. we can do A/B rollouts at the routing layer so only a percentage of traffic uses a quantized variant during validation.
19:00 Lara Chen: what about fallbacks — if dedicated hits saturation, do you have auto-fallback to hosted?
19:12 Maya Thompson: yes we support policy-based fallback: overflow to hosted or to a smaller model variant. that's part of the graceful degradation playbook.
20:00 Diego Ramos: show me the math on cost per 1M tokens for dedicated vs hosted for our profile — can you approximate now?
20:12 Maya Thompson: quick approximations: hosted at this scale — say $9–12 per million tokens depending on model; dedicated blended might be $6–8 per million once you amortize committed capacity and realize batching gains — these are illustrative. we'll provide concrete numbers in the spreadsheet.
21:30 Lara Chen: okay that helps.
22:00 Priya Nair: are there any security pre-reqs for a pilot?
22:12 Maya Thompson: basic NDA + data handling addendum if you want to route PII. we also provide SOC2 and can enable VPC peering for dedicated/pvt for direct network connections.
23:00 Ethan Park: tech follow-up — Diego, if you can export a week of traffic histograms (tokens/request, concurrency), I can use that to size dedicated capacity and simulate batching windows.
23:30 Diego Ramos: will do.
24:00 Lara Chen: slightly worried about the 95th/99th tail though — how do you guarantee SLOs?
24:15 Ethan Park: we support per-route SLOs and monitoring. runtime will prioritize low-latency shards and you can set a multi-tiered policy: hot small-batches for SLO-critical routes, cold large-batches for low-priority traffic. redundancy and spillover policies preserve availability.
25:00 Maya Thompson: recap: we will send pilot pricing spreadsheet, SOC2 copy, and an SOW template; Ethan will run a cache/batching sim after you share prompts and traffic patterns; schedule a technical deep dive to lock down sizing and an SLO plan.
26:00 Priya Nair: procurement asks that the SOW include termination, liability limits, and data handling specifics.
26:20 Maya Thompson: noted — we'll include standard clauses.
27:00 Lara Chen: any questions from you, Diego?
27:10 Diego Ramos: just one — do you have metrics around median vs p95 improvement with KV cache on production customers?
27:30 Ethan Park: yes, on customers with heavy static system prompts we've seen billed tokens drop 25–60% and CPU/GPU usage go down 10–30% depending on model and cache hit rate. I'll share anonymized charts.
28:00 Lara Chen: nice. ok let's move to next steps and rough dates.
28:10 Maya Thompson: I'll email the pilot pack by Friday (2026-10-02). Ethan will start the sim once prompts are shared, target results by 2026-10-04. Follow-up technical deep dive 2026-10-06 (tentative).
29:00 Priya Nair: procurement will try to have initial list by 2026-10-05.
30:00 Maya Thompson: great. anything else?
30:15 Lara Chen: just — include regression checks for accuracy when you propose quantization options.
30:30 Ethan Park: yes we'll include eval thresholds and rollback gates.
31:00 Maya Thompson: thanks everyone. we'll send notes, pilot pricing, SOC2, and schedule.
47:00 Meeting close

Action item recap: see action_items above.
